items.title: CVE-2026-105192 — LMCache: Remote code execution via unsafe deserialization in multiprocess mode transport
items.body:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-105192 affectant lmcache (pip) (score CVSS 9.8).

LMCache: Remote code execution via unsafe deserialization in multiprocess mode transport

LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. The intended clients are sibling LMCache processes. There is no CURVE, ZAP, password, or message authentication on that socket. LMCache used only inside a vLLM process does not open this port.
items.detail:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-105192 affectant lmcache (pip) (score CVSS 9.8).

LMCache: Remote code execution via unsafe deserialization in multiprocess mode transport

LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. The intended clients are sibling LMCache processes. There is no CURVE, ZAP, password, or message authentication on that socket. LMCache used only inside a vLLM process does not open this port. The transport binds to localhost unless the operator sets a routable address with --host, which is how multi-node deployments let peers connect. The 9.8 score is for that routable configuration. A stock single-host install that leaves the default bind is not reachable from other machines.

Messages on the socket are msgpack. Extension code 1 is registered for DeviceIPCWrapper and is passed to DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize in lmcache/v1/platform/base/ipc_wrapper.py, which calls pickle.loads. That hook runs from ext_hook in lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py while the server is still decoding REGISTER_KV_CACHE arguments, before the handler runs. A single unauthenticated ZMQ DEALER message to the transport port (default 5555) therefore executes code as the user the LMCache process runs as. Official container images run that process as root.

The decode path shipped in v0.3.9. It is still present in the latest PyPI release, v0.5.5, in the v0.5.6 release candidates through v0.5.6rc3, and on the dev branch as of 2026-10-07. No fixed version has been published.

This is the documented multi-node setting. The ZMQ transport listens on port 5555.

python -m lmcache.v1.multiprocess.http_server \ --http-host 127.0.0.1 --http-port 8080 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5555 \ -

items.detail:
Vulnérabilité élevée CVE-2026-84316 affectant github.com/0xJacky/Nginx-UI (go) (score CVSS 8.8).

Nginx UI: nginx config directive denylist (ValidateConfigFile) is bypassable via same-line ";" separation → authenticated directive injection (RCE on the official image)

This is distinct from the config_add gap (the MCP nginx_config_add tool not calling the validator at all): here the validator IS called and still bypassed, so fixing config_add does not fix this.

Authenticated with a node secret ( X-Node-Secret , from nginx-ui's first-boot log) or a user JWT. Every step below hits a path that calls ValidateConfigFile.

Authenticated config-injection that defeats the directive-validation control on all guarded write paths. On deployments with njs/perl available (the official Docker image ships ngx_http_js_module.so): code execution in the nginx worker and, via user root , arbitrary file read/write as root (trivially escalated to full host compromise). On stock nginx without those modules: reliable DoS (failed reload) plus user root privilege regression.

Do not hand-roll a newline/first-token denylist. Validate the way nginx parses: split statements on ; (and handle blocks, comments, line continuations), validate EVERY statement, block/limit include , and recurse into included files — or validate via an allowlist and/or by running nginx -t on the candidate before activating it.

Distinct from CVE-2026-33032 (unauthenticated MCP endpoint — an auth issue, now fixed) and from the separately reported config_add validation gap (a missing validator call on one path). This is a bypass of the validator itself, affecting every path that calls it; no existing CVE/GHSA covers it (checked osv.dev and the GitHub advisory database for this repo). Appears novel.

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

Anne Arundel County, Maryland, said an intruder stole files from government systems, and investigators are working to assess how much data was exposed.

Officials in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, confirmed that hackers stole files from government systems during an incident in August.

A county spokesperson told Recorded Future News that they discovered “irregular activity” on August 28 and began an investigation on a “limited subset of systems within the county computer network.”

“Through the course of the county’s response and investigation, it was determined that an unauthorized actor gained access to a limited number of systems and copied certain files from those systems,” the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson did not respond to questions about what data was involved but said investigators are currently reviewing the files to determine whether any stolen information related to residents of the county.

The Baltimore suburb is home to more than 600,000 residents and the state’s capital of Annapolis. Washington, D.C. is nearby, as well. Dozens of federal agencies have offices or headquarters in the county, including the Defense Department, the Internal Revenue Service, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Social Security Administration, the Department of Agriculture, the U.S. Coast Guard and more.

County officials said they notified federal law enforcement about the data breach as well as other government agencies.

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par Unit 42.

Our analysis an AI-powered espionage campaign targeting government Linux infrastructure with custom malware, web shells, and advanced credential theft.

Unit 42 identified a campaign targeting government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, with observed activity spanning from October 2025–April 2026. We track this activity as CL-UNK-1211.

In the operations we witnessed, the attackers relied on AI-generated payloads. Multiple artifacts deployed throughout the intrusion contained AI-made conversational annotations and developer reasoning comments, suggesting that the code was either generated using large language models (LLMs) or executed by an automated AI agent.

The attackers behind this cluster of activity focused on Linux environments to conduct extensive reconnaissance and maintain persistent network access to support intelligence-gathering. The attackers attempted to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to access social media accounts.

The campaign included a diverse toolkit that combined open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors and widespread web shell deployments. We observed various defense evasion techniques, including attempts to disable endpoint protections, erase system logs and plant deceptive red-team markers to disguise activity as a legitimate security assessment.

Our attribution of this activity to CL-UNK-1211 is in accordance with the Unit 42 attribution framework . We designate the term UNK to clusters of activity whose affiliation with either nation-state or cybercrime activity we have not yet determined.

This investigation uncovers the defining tools, techniques and attack patterns of this activity cluster.

Unit 42 dissects a cyberattack targeting a European bank's IT infrastructure, delivering concrete defense strategies to help organizations detect and counter comparable threats.

When unusual activity was detected on a European bank’s central IT system, its internal security team quickly recognized that the incident warranted immediate response. They discovered unauthorized VPN-based access attempts that spanned several months. They then engaged Unit 42 to determine the full scope of the intrusion, identify any persistent footholds and secure the environment.

While the activity appeared to be a stealthy cyberespionage campaign, the actual intrusion was made possible by gaps in foundational security controls. Rather than relying on novel techniques, the threat actor succeeded through persistence, exploiting weaknesses that stronger identity protections and basic security hygiene could have prevented. The case highlights an important lesson: Sometimes the most damaging intrusions begin with the simplest oversights.

The intrusion originated through a third-party-managed external gateway appliance that was not properly configured to enforce strict authentication. The threat actor conducted multiple rounds of reconnaissance, performing extensive host and network scans across a wide range of protocols and interacting with thousands of systems. items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Hacker News.

ConnectWise disabled seven application identities and suspended Cloud Backup after attackers compromised Microsoft 365 tenants.

ConnectWise on Saturday said it has disabled seven ConnectWise application identities as it continues its investigation into an incident in which unknown threat actors obtained unauthorized access to the application identities and compromised Microsoft 365 tenants.

The IT management software provider said it took the action on October 17, 2026, at 07:00 UTC, adding it has also suspended Cloud Backup service by revoking certificates used for affected application connections across all users.

"Disabling the affected connections prevents new authentication through those connections; it does not reverse changes previously made inside a tenant," it said.

"The affected shared Cloud Backup credentials are no longer valid. Previously issued access tokens may remain usable until they expire or are otherwise invalidated. Any unauthorized credentials, permissions, or other access established through separate identities require additional review and remediation."

ConnectWise also noted that scheduled backups are not running, and access to affected backup archives and restoration capabilities remains unavailable. However, it emphasized that existing archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, and that there is no evidence they were breached or accessed by the attackers.

Out of an abundance of caution, the company said it has temporarily taken SaaS Security and Cloud Management offline while it completes its review of the incident.

Attention au chiffre : il ne s’agit pas de 1,48 million de personnes. Les enregistrements correspondent essentiellement à des fiches de chiens enregistrés dans les bases de la Centrale Canine , auxquelles sont associées des informations sur leurs éleveurs. ChimeraZ annonce notamment 39 893 adresses email .

Le hacker ChimeraZ affirme avoir récupéré une partie de la base de Zabun , avec 1 571 596 lignes concernant 892 288 personnes .

La base, proposée à la vente le 17 octobre 2026 , pèserait 3,8 Go . ChimeraZ revendique notamment 430 587 numéros de téléphone uniques et 177 023 adresses email différentes .

Zabun développe des logiciels CRM, sites web et outils destinés aux professionnels de l’immobilier. L’entreprise, filiale de Zimmo, se présente comme le plus important fournisseur de logiciels immobiliers en Belgique depuis l’acquisition de Skarabee en 2023.

Son logiciel centralise les biens, les contacts, les prospects, les rendez-vous, l’historique des communications et les documents liés aux dossiers immobiliers. Autrement dit, une compromission à ce niveau peut dépasser très largement les seules coordonnées d’utilisateurs de Zabun.

Cyberattaque.org s’est procuré un exemple des données diffusées par ChimeraZ. Celui-ci correspond à un document généré depuis l’environnement Zabun et consacré à un bien immobilier.

Le fichier contient les caractéristiques détaillées du logement, son prix, son adresse, des références cadastrales, mais également les noms de personnes intéressées, leurs numéros de téléphone, adresses email, adresses postales et l’historique des échanges avec l’agence .

items.title: Measuring Human Cryptanalysis Effort
items.body:
Signal de veille — Schneier on Sec..

Matthew Green has a new site that tries to estimate the number of cryptanalyst-hours that have been spent analyzing different public-key algorithms: Abstract: We estimate how much public cryptanalysis each public-key assumption has received, using the literature itself as the instrument.
items.detail:
Signal de veille — Schneier on Sec..

Matthew Green has a new site that tries to estimate the number of cryptanalyst-hours that have been spent analyzing different public-key algorithms: Abstract: We estimate how much public cryptanalysis each public-key assumption has received, using the literature itself as the instrument. From roughly sixteen thousand candidate papers we classify cryptanalytic work on ECDLP, structured and plain lattices, syndrome decoding and their comparators, then convert papers into estimated research-allocation years through a person-level author map. These publication-based estimates may substantially overstate actual time spent. Lattices have overtaken elliptic curves in this cumulative measure only recently; we express that history as inference budgets under stated productivity assumptions. The study was conducted by AI models: Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 built the pipeline, ran the analysis and wrote this page, with contributions from GPT-6 Astra. Matthew Green set the questions, made the key methodological decisions and oversaw the work. There are a lot of caveats to this analysis. It relies on published work, so anything unpublished does not count. This includes both academic cryptanalysis that didn’t result in a paper, and intelligence agency cryptanalysis done in secret. But it’s a good first stab at a metric of this sort.

« Développer une offre de services IaaS, PaaS et d’intelligence artificielle répondant aux standards les plus exigeants de sécurité et de souveraineté juridique.» C’est pour ce projet que Cloud Temple a été sélectionné dans le cadre de l’appel « Renforcement de l’offre de services cloud « . L’entreprise mène un consortium qui rassemble Thales, Bull, Vates et le CEA. L’appel est opéré par Bpifrance pour le compte de l’État. Lancé en mars 2024, cet appel à projets prolonge la stratégie cloud de France 2030. Il vise à renforcer l’offre française et européenne de services cloud au service de la souveraineté numérique et de l’IA. Nous en reprenons néanmoins quelques-uns, en particulier parce qu’ils illustrent un état de fait : pour une même chose, tout le monde ne paye pas le même prix. 7 Md€ à aller chercher en négociant ?… L’analyse couvre la période de juin 2025 à juin 2026. Elle englobe 2568 entreprises actives. La majorité en France (60,5 %). Le reste dans 13 autres pays, principalement l’Allemagne (16 %) et le Royaume-Uni (12,6 %). La distribution est à l’image du marché européen : 91 % de ces entreprises comptent moins de 250 employés. À partir de cet échantillon, Spendesk extrapole à l’UE en s’appuyant sur les données d’Eurostat pour 2024. Keyrus nomme Nicolas Bouffard au poste de Directeur Général France. Rattaché à Marc Stukkens, Directeur Général du Groupe Keyrus, il prend la responsabilité des activités françaises du groupe, qui réunissent près de 600 collaborateurs autour de quatre domaines : Data & AI, Business Transformation, Software Engineering et Cybersecurity. Diplômé de l’EPITA et de la Cranfield School of Management, Nicolas Bouffard totalise plus de vingt ans d’expérience dans la technologie et le conseil. Il a occupé des fonctions commerciales et managériales chez Oracle et SAP, avant de diriger les activités franciliennes d’Akkodis, puis les activités Cloud en France de Devoteam, sur les écosystèmes Microsoft, AWS et Google. Sa feuille de route s’articule autour de quatre priorités : accélérer une croissance rentable, renforcer le go-to-market sectoriel et les grands comptes, transformer les offres et les compétences à l’ère de l’IA, et construire un modèle unifié, « One Keyrus France ».
